**Jontay Porter** ([/ˈ dʒ ɒ n t eɪ/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")[_JON-tay_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key");[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-1) born November 15, 1999) is an American professional [basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basketball "Basketball") player for the [Seattle Super Hawks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle_Super_Hawks?action=edit&redlink=1 "Seattle Super Hawks (page does not exist)") of the [USBL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Basketball_League_(2026) "United States Basketball League (2026)"). Porter was banned for life by the [National Basketball Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Basketball_Association "National Basketball Association") (NBA) in 2024 for violating their [gambling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gambling "Gambling") policies while playing for the [Toronto Raptors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto_Raptors "Toronto Raptors"). The scandal resulted in him facing criminal charges, for which he pled guilty.

Porter played [college basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_basketball "College basketball") for the [Missouri Tigers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri_Tigers_men's_basketball "Missouri Tigers men's basketball") where he played alongside his older brother, [Michael Porter Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Porter_Jr. "Michael Porter Jr.") He was awarded as the [Southeastern Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference "Southeastern Conference") Sixth Man of the Year during his freshman season. Porter was an early entrant in the [2019 NBA draft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_NBA_draft "2019 NBA draft") but went unselected, and started his professional career in 2020 on a [two-way contract](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-way_contract "Two-way contract") with the [Memphis Grizzlies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memphis_Grizzlies "Memphis Grizzlies") and spent time with their [NBA G League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_G_League "NBA G League") affiliate [Memphis Hustle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memphis_Hustle "Memphis Hustle"). He sat out the 2021–22 season after he was waived by Memphis. Porter joined the [Wisconsin Herd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin_Herd "Wisconsin Herd") of the G League for the 2022–23 season, and after starting the 2023–24 season with the G League's [Motor City Cruise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motor_City_Cruise "Motor City Cruise"), Porter was signed by the Toronto Raptors on a two-way contract with the [Raptors 905](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raptors_905 "Raptors 905").

## High school career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jontay_Porter&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: High school career")]

Much like his older brother [Michael](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Porter_Jr. "Michael Porter Jr."), Porter started out his high school career playing for [Father Tolton Regional Catholic High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Father_Tolton_Regional_Catholic_High_School "Father Tolton Regional Catholic High School") in their home town of [Columbia, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia,_Missouri "Columbia, Missouri"). In his freshman year, he averaged 11.8 points and 7.8 rebounds per game for Father Tolton before being a key figure in helping them win the Missouri Class 3 State Championship for the first time during his sophomore season. In his junior year of high school, Porter and Michael, along with their younger brother Coban, moved to [Seattle, Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle,_Washington "Seattle, Washington"), after his father earned an assistant coaching job at the [University of Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Washington "University of Washington") for their basketball team. During Porter's and Michael's time at [Nathan Hale High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathan_Hale_High_School_(Washington) "Nathan Hale High School (Washington)"), the brothers were coached by former [NBA All-Star](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_All-Star "NBA All-Star")[Brandon Roy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brandon_Roy "Brandon Roy"), who helped lead the squad to a perfect 29–0 record and the Washington Class 3A State Championship. Under the coaching of Roy, Porter averaged a double-double of 14.3 points and 13.6 rebounds per game for Nathan Hale High School, thus earning a name for himself alongside his older brother.

Porter was previously a recruit under the Class of 2018, with him being ranked as high as 11th overall by [ESPN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESPN "ESPN") at one point.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-2) However, after his father was hired as an assistant coach for the [University of Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Missouri "University of Missouri"), his older brother changed his commitment from the [University of Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Washington "University of Washington") to his hometown University of Missouri, and [Brandon Roy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brandon_Roy "Brandon Roy") changed coaching positions from Nathan Hale to [Garfield High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garfield_High_School_(Seattle) "Garfield High School (Seattle)"), Porter [reclassified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reclassification_(education) "Reclassification (education)") himself into the Class of 2017 alongside his brother, joining his family out at the University of Missouri. Between his time preparing for his transfer from high school into college, Porter grew two more inches, thus allowing him to play as a power forward, with center being a viable possibility as well.

## College career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jontay_Porter&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: College career")]

Porter, five days before his 18th birthday, made his season debut on November 10, 2017, in a 74–59 win over [Iowa State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iowa_State_Cyclones_men's_basketball "Iowa State Cyclones men's basketball"). Three days after his debut, he recorded 11 points and 8 rebounds in a blowout 99–55 win over [Wagner College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wagner_College "Wagner College"). One week later, Porter recorded his first collegiate double-double with 11 points and 11 rebounds in a 67–62 win over [Emporia State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emporia_State_University "Emporia State University"). On January 10, 2018, Porter made his first start of the season for Missouri, recording a double-double of 15 points and 10 rebounds in a 68–56 win over the [University of Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_Bulldogs_men's_basketball "Georgia Bulldogs men's basketball").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-3) Porter continued starting for the team during the next five games before returning to the bench for the rest of the season. On February 27, Porter scored a season-high 24 points to go with a team-leading 7 rebounds and 6 assists in a 74–66 win over [Vanderbilt University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanderbilt_Commodores_men's_basketball "Vanderbilt Commodores men's basketball"). In his last game of the season, he started for Missouri in the NCAA Tournament. On April 5, Porter announced he would enter the [2018 NBA draft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_NBA_draft "2018 NBA draft") alongside his brother. However, unlike [Michael Porter Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Porter_Jr. "Michael Porter Jr."), he entered the draft without hiring an agent first, thus allowing him the possibility to return to Missouri for another year if he was willing to do so.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-4) On the May 30 draft day deadline, Porter decided to return to Missouri instead of entering the NBA Draft early where he was seen as a likely first round pick, possibly joining his brother Michael in the lottery had he stayed in. Porter was seen as potential lottery pick for the [2019 NBA draft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_NBA_draft "2019 NBA draft").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-5)

On October 21, 2018, it was announced that Porter would miss his sophomore season after tearing both the ACL and MCL in his right knee during a scrimmage.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-6) While rehabilitating, Porter tore his ACL again on March 23, 2019.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-7) Despite the injury and Porter's stock plummeting, Porter entered his name for the [2019 NBA draft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_NBA_draft "2019 NBA draft") as one of 233 early-entrant participants.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-9) Porter was also one of 66 original participants included in the 2019 [NBA Draft Combine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_Draft_Combine "NBA Draft Combine").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-10) 89 players removed their names from draft consideration at the May 30 deadline, but Porter chose to remain eligible in the 2019 NBA draft's entry pool.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-11) After his injuries, Porter was seen as a late first round or second round pick.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-12)

### Memphis Grizzlies (2020–2021)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jontay_Porter&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Memphis Grizzlies (2020–2021)")]

Porter was not chosen in the [2019 NBA draft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_NBA_draft "2019 NBA draft"), partially due to teams wary of his injury history.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-13) On March 8, 2020, Porter signed with the [Memphis Grizzlies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memphis_Grizzlies "Memphis Grizzlies").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-15) During his rookie season's free agency period, Porter was reported to have been granted access to a VIP account on [FanDuel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FanDuel "FanDuel") due to him already having a habit of [Wall Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wall_Street "Wall Street") day trading and [cryptocurrency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptocurrency "Cryptocurrency") investments, though this would not come to light until 2025.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-TorontoLife-16) On November 22, 2020, the [Memphis Grizzlies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memphis_Grizzlies "Memphis Grizzlies") announced that they had re-signed Porter, this time to a multi-year contract.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-17) On July 30, 2021, he was waived by the Grizzlies after making 11 appearances.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-18) Porter joined the [Denver Nuggets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denver_Nuggets "Denver Nuggets") for the [2022 NBA Summer League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_NBA_Summer_League "2022 NBA Summer League").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-19)

### Gambling charges and ban from NBA

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jontay_Porter&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Gambling charges and ban from NBA")]

On March 25, 2024, ESPN reported that the NBA had opened an investigation of Porter for "multiple instances of betting irregularities over the past several months".[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-26) On April 11, the [Colorado Division of Gaming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_Department_of_Revenue "Colorado Department of Revenue") issued an instruction to state sportsbook operators to immediately report any potential wagering on "NBA affiliated games" by accounts connected to Porter.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-27) The investigation centered on irregularities found related to [proposition bets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proposition_bet "Proposition bet") around Porter's individual statistics.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-:1-28)

It subsequently emerged that Porter was finding it difficult to service significant gambling debts. His right knee had never fully recovered from the severe injury he'd suffered at Missouri, making it harder for him to catch on in the NBA. Soon after arriving in Toronto, he used a friend's phone to secretly bet on NBA games; while he netted modest profits, they were still not enough to pay off his earlier debts. By the winter of 2024, he had amassed a particularly large debt to Brooklyn gambler Ammar Awawdeh; according to a post-mortem by _[Toronto Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto\_Life "Toronto Life"),_ the debt was large enough that Awawdeh could potentially "end (Porter's) career in an instant." Using this leverage, Awadeh pressed Porter into performing a number of "specials" for Awawdeh and four of his friends–Long Phi "Bruce" Pham, Shane Hennen, Timothy McCormack, and Mahmoud Mollah. Porter took part in a scheme to help Awawdeh and his friends win proposition bets tied to Porter's performance. Awawdeh and his co-conspirators would bet that Porter would fall short of certain benchmarks. Porter then feigned injury to leave games early, ensuring the bets would hit.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-TorontoLife-16)

The scheme unraveled during the Raptors' March 20 game against the [Sacramento Kings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacramento_Kings "Sacramento Kings"), a game on which Porter bet that his own team would lose. According to the NBA, Porter told Awawdeh, Pham, and Mollah in a secret [Telegram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegram_(software) "Telegram (software)") channel that he intended to feign illness again. He had laid the groundwork for doing so the previous week by complaining about food poisoning.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-:1-28)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-TorontoLife-16) While at the [Resorts Casino Hotel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resorts_Casino_Hotel "Resorts Casino Hotel") in [Atlantic City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_City "Atlantic City") with Awawdeh, McCormack, and Pham, Mollah then used his account with [DraftKings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DraftKings "DraftKings")' [sportsbook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportsbook "Sportsbook") at the casino to wager $80,000 on a [parlay bet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parlay "Parlay") that Porter would not meet certain player statistics – an [under bet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Over%E2%80%93under "Over–under") – which would have won $1.1 million. Porter, Awawdeh, Pham, and Mollah would have each received 24 percent of the proceeds had the bet hit, while McCormack would have gotten the rest. Porter's behavior drew notice once he removed himself from the game due to illness. The size of the bet was highly irregular given Porter's relatively low stature. The low odds also raised suspicion. After an independent monitor flagged the bet, DraftKings refused to pay out and froze Mollah's account. Internal investigations by FanDuel and DraftKings revealed other suspicious bets Mollah placed on Porter's performance, including a January 26 game against the [Los Angeles Clippers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Clippers "Los Angeles Clippers") in which Porter feigned an eye injury. It was the largest payout of the night, as was the March 20 game. DraftKings and FanDuel reported their findings to the NBA and the [International Betting Integrity Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Betting_Integrity_Association?action=edit&redlink=1 "International Betting Integrity Association (page does not exist)"). The [FBI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Bureau_of_Investigation "Federal Bureau of Investigation") was called in as well.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-NBALifetimeBan-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-:0-30)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-TorontoLife-16) In its investigation, the NBA also found that between January and March 2024, Porter had placed 13 bets on NBA games using another person's account. Some of the wagers included parlay bets involving the Raptors losing. His wagers totaled $54,000 over that period, netting over $22,000 in winnings.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-:1-28) The NBA accused him of "disclosing confidential information to sports bettors, limiting his own participation in one or more games for betting purposes, and betting on NBA games".[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-:0-30)

On April 17, Porter was [banned for life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_people_banned_or_suspended_by_the_NBA "List of people banned or suspended by the NBA") from further play or any other involvement in the NBA and its associated leagues.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-NBALifetimeBan-29)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-espn-lifetime-ban-31) He became the first active player to be banned for gambling since [Jack Molinas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Molinas "Jack Molinas") in 1954,[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-:1-28) as well as the first active player to be permanently banned from the NBA without any means to return since [Richard Dumas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Dumas "Richard Dumas") in 1996.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-32) On June 4, 2024, Pham was arrested at [JFK International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy_International_Airport "John F. Kennedy International Airport") while attempting to flee the country.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-33) McCormack, Mollad, and Awawdeh were subsequently taken into custody as well.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-34) On July 3, Porter was also charged with a federal felony in relation to the case involving those four men.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-35) On July 3, 2024, court papers were made public revealing Porter's imminent criminal charges in the United States at the federal level for his role in the sports betting scandal.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-criminalfacing-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-37) Porter is also undergoing a criminal investigation in Canada.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-criminalfacing-36)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-38) In the federal case on July 10, Porter would plead guilty to a charge of conspiracy to commit wire fraud, which could impose a range of no time in prison to up to 20 years in prison for what he did, but faces a most likely time of 41 to 51 months in prison.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-39) One of the conditions related to his guilty plea was to forfeit his passport for a pre-sentence release, which forbade him to play overseas for the [Promitheas Patras B.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Promitheas_Patras_B.C. "Promitheas Patras B.C.") of the [Greek Basketball League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_Basketball_League "Greek Basketball League").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-40) The NBA would also implement what is called the "Jontay Porter Rule" following his ban, which forbade sportsbooks from including unders on player props who are on either [two-way contracts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-way_contract "Two-way contract") or 10-day contracts.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-41)

## Post-ban basketball career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jontay_Porter&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Post-ban basketball career")]

### Seattle Super Hawks (2026–present)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jontay_Porter&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Seattle Super Hawks (2026–present)")]

On February 25, 2026, over a year after presumably serving his original sentence in the USA and close to over two years after first being permanently banned by the NBA, Porter signed a contract to join the Seattle Super Hawks for the 2026 version of the [United States Basketball League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Basketball_League_(2026) "United States Basketball League (2026)").[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-42)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-43)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-44) He made his debut with Seattle on March 7, producing a [triple-double](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triple-double "Triple-double") of 21 points, 14 rebounds, and 14 assists, alongside three blocks and two steals in a 111–88 win over the Lilac City Legends.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-45) Porter would not only help the Super Hawks get to a nearly undefeated season, but he'd also lead them to their first ever championship in the league's inaugural season as well.

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jontay_Porter&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Personal life")]

In addition to his older brother [Michael Porter Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Porter_Jr. "Michael Porter Jr.") with the [Brooklyn Nets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn_Nets "Brooklyn Nets"), Jontay has two older sisters, Bri and Cierra, both of whom were deemed medically retired from playing sports, both due to multiple leg injuries.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-46) Cierra Porter later returned for her senior year at the [University of Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri_Tigers_women's_basketball "Missouri Tigers women's basketball").[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-47) Two of Porter's younger brothers, Coban and Jevon, played collegiate basketball as well, with Coban previously playing for the [University of Denver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Denver "University of Denver") and Jevon currently playing for [Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri_Tigers_men's_basketball "Missouri Tigers men's basketball") after he previously for [Pepperdine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pepperdine_Waves_men's_basketball "Pepperdine Waves men's basketball") for two seasons and [Loyola Marymount](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loyola_Marymount_Lions_men's_basketball "Loyola Marymount Lions men's basketball") for the [2024–25 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024%E2%80%9325_NCAA_Division_I_men's_basketball_season "2024–25 NCAA Division I men's basketball season").[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-48)

Porter and his wife had their first child in November 2024.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-49)

**Jontay Porter** ([/ˈ dʒ ɒ n t eɪ/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")[_JON-tay_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key");[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-1) born November 15, 1999) is an American professional [basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basketball "Basketball") player for the [Seattle Super Hawks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle_Super_Hawks?action=edit&redlink=1 "Seattle Super Hawks (page does not exist)") of the [USBL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Basketball_League_(2026) "United States Basketball League (2026)"). Porter was banned for life by the [National Basketball Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Basketball_Association "National Basketball Association") (NBA) in 2024 for violating their [gambling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gambling "Gambling") policies while playing for the [Toronto Raptors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto_Raptors "Toronto Raptors"). The scandal resulted in him facing criminal charges, for which he pled guilty.

Porter played [college basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_basketball "College basketball") for the [Missouri Tigers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri_Tigers_men's_basketball "Missouri Tigers men's basketball") where he played alongside his older brother, [Michael Porter Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Porter_Jr. "Michael Porter Jr.") He was awarded as the [Southeastern Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference "Southeastern Conference") Sixth Man of the Year during his freshman season. Porter was an early entrant in the [2019 NBA draft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_NBA_draft "2019 NBA draft") but went unselected, and started his professional career in 2020 on a [two-way contract](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-way_contract "Two-way contract") with the [Memphis Grizzlies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memphis_Grizzlies "Memphis Grizzlies") and spent time with their [NBA G League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_G_League "NBA G League") affiliate [Memphis Hustle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memphis_Hustle "Memphis Hustle"). He sat out the 2021–22 season after he was waived by Memphis. Porter joined the [Wisconsin Herd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin_Herd "Wisconsin Herd") of the G League for the 2022–23 season, and after starting the 2023–24 season with the G League's [Motor City Cruise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motor_City_Cruise "Motor City Cruise"), Porter was signed by the Toronto Raptors on a two-way contract with the [Raptors 905](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raptors_905 "Raptors 905").

## High school career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jontay_Porter&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: High school career")]

Much like his older brother [Michael](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Porter_Jr. "Michael Porter Jr."), Porter started out his high school career playing for [Father Tolton Regional Catholic High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Father_Tolton_Regional_Catholic_High_School "Father Tolton Regional Catholic High School") in their home town of [Columbia, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia,_Missouri "Columbia, Missouri"). In his freshman year, he averaged 11.8 points and 7.8 rebounds per game for Father Tolton before being a key figure in helping them win the Missouri Class 3 State Championship for the first time during his sophomore season. In his junior year of high school, Porter and Michael, along with their younger brother Coban, moved to [Seattle, Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle,_Washington "Seattle, Washington"), after his father earned an assistant coaching job at the [University of Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Washington "University of Washington") for their basketball team. During Porter's and Michael's time at [Nathan Hale High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathan_Hale_High_School_(Washington) "Nathan Hale High School (Washington)"), the brothers were coached by former [NBA All-Star](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_All-Star "NBA All-Star")[Brandon Roy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brandon_Roy "Brandon Roy"), who helped lead the squad to a perfect 29–0 record and the Washington Class 3A State Championship. Under the coaching of Roy, Porter averaged a double-double of 14.3 points and 13.6 rebounds per game for Nathan Hale High School, thus earning a name for himself alongside his older brother.

Porter was previously a recruit under the Class of 2018, with him being ranked as high as 11th overall by [ESPN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESPN "ESPN") at one point.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-2) However, after his father was hired as an assistant coach for the [University of Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Missouri "University of Missouri"), his older brother changed his commitment from the [University of Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Washington "University of Washington") to his hometown University of Missouri, and [Brandon Roy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brandon_Roy "Brandon Roy") changed coaching positions from Nathan Hale to [Garfield High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garfield_High_School_(Seattle) "Garfield High School (Seattle)"), Porter [reclassified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reclassification_(education) "Reclassification (education)") himself into the Class of 2017 alongside his brother, joining his family out at the University of Missouri. Between his time preparing for his transfer from high school into college, Porter grew two more inches, thus allowing him to play as a power forward, with center being a viable possibility as well.

## College career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jontay_Porter&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: College career")]

Porter, five days before his 18th birthday, made his season debut on November 10, 2017, in a 74–59 win over [Iowa State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iowa_State_Cyclones_men's_basketball "Iowa State Cyclones men's basketball"). Three days after his debut, he recorded 11 points and 8 rebounds in a blowout 99–55 win over [Wagner College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wagner_College "Wagner College"). One week later, Porter recorded his first collegiate double-double with 11 points and 11 rebounds in a 67–62 win over [Emporia State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emporia_State_University "Emporia State University"). On January 10, 2018, Porter made his first start of the season for Missouri, recording a double-double of 15 points and 10 rebounds in a 68–56 win over the [University of Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_Bulldogs_men's_basketball "Georgia Bulldogs men's basketball").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-3) Porter continued starting for the team during the next five games before returning to the bench for the rest of the season. On February 27, Porter scored a season-high 24 points to go with a team-leading 7 rebounds and 6 assists in a 74–66 win over [Vanderbilt University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanderbilt_Commodores_men's_basketball "Vanderbilt Commodores men's basketball"). In his last game of the season, he started for Missouri in the NCAA Tournament. On April 5, Porter announced he would enter the [2018 NBA draft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_NBA_draft "2018 NBA draft") alongside his brother. However, unlike [Michael Porter Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Porter_Jr. "Michael Porter Jr."), he entered the draft without hiring an agent first, thus allowing him the possibility to return to Missouri for another year if he was willing to do so.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-4) On the May 30 draft day deadline, Porter decided to return to Missouri instead of entering the NBA Draft early where he was seen as a likely first round pick, possibly joining his brother Michael in the lottery had he stayed in. Porter was seen as potential lottery pick for the [2019 NBA draft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_NBA_draft "2019 NBA draft").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-5)

On October 21, 2018, it was announced that Porter would miss his sophomore season after tearing both the ACL and MCL in his right knee during a scrimmage.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-6) While rehabilitating, Porter tore his ACL again on March 23, 2019.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-7) Despite the injury and Porter's stock plummeting, Porter entered his name for the [2019 NBA draft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_NBA_draft "2019 NBA draft") as one of 233 early-entrant participants.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-9) Porter was also one of 66 original participants included in the 2019 [NBA Draft Combine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_Draft_Combine "NBA Draft Combine").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-10) 89 players removed their names from draft consideration at the May 30 deadline, but Porter chose to remain eligible in the 2019 NBA draft's entry pool.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-11) After his injuries, Porter was seen as a late first round or second round pick.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-12)

## Professional career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jontay_Porter&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Professional career")]

### Memphis Grizzlies (2020–2021)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jontay_Porter&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Memphis Grizzlies (2020–2021)")]

Porter was not chosen in the [2019 NBA draft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_NBA_draft "2019 NBA draft"), partially due to teams wary of his injury history.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-13) On March 8, 2020, Porter signed with the [Memphis Grizzlies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memphis_Grizzlies "Memphis Grizzlies").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-15) During his rookie season's free agency period, Porter was reported to have been granted access to a VIP account on [FanDuel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FanDuel "FanDuel") due to him already having a habit of [Wall Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wall_Street "Wall Street") day trading and [cryptocurrency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptocurrency "Cryptocurrency") investments, though this would not come to light until 2025.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-TorontoLife-16) On November 22, 2020, the [Memphis Grizzlies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memphis_Grizzlies "Memphis Grizzlies") announced that they had re-signed Porter, this time to a multi-year contract.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-17) On July 30, 2021, he was waived by the Grizzlies after making 11 appearances.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-18) Porter joined the [Denver Nuggets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denver_Nuggets "Denver Nuggets") for the [2022 NBA Summer League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_NBA_Summer_League "2022 NBA Summer League").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-19)

### Wisconsin Herd (2022–2023)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jontay_Porter&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Wisconsin Herd (2022–2023)")]

On November 3, 2022, Porter was named to the opening night roster of the [Wisconsin Herd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin_Herd "Wisconsin Herd"), the G League team affiliated with the [Milwaukee Bucks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milwaukee_Bucks "Milwaukee Bucks").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-20)

### Motor City Cruise (2023)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jontay_Porter&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Motor City Cruise (2023)")]

On December 9, 2023, Porter signed a [two-way contract](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-way_contract "Two-way contract") with the [Toronto Raptors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto_Raptors "Toronto Raptors").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-24) He averaged 4.4 points, 3.2 rebounds and 2.3 assists in 26 games played.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-25)

### Gambling charges and ban from NBA

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jontay_Porter&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Gambling charges and ban from NBA")]

On March 25, 2024, ESPN reported that the NBA had opened an investigation of Porter for "multiple instances of betting irregularities over the past several months".[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-26) On April 11, the [Colorado Division of Gaming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_Department_of_Revenue "Colorado Department of Revenue") issued an instruction to state sportsbook operators to immediately report any potential wagering on "NBA affiliated games" by accounts connected to Porter.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-27) The investigation centered on irregularities found related to [proposition bets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proposition_bet "Proposition bet") around Porter's individual statistics.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-:1-28)

It subsequently emerged that Porter was finding it difficult to service significant gambling debts. His right knee had never fully recovered from the severe injury he'd suffered at Missouri, making it harder for him to catch on in the NBA. Soon after arriving in Toronto, he used a friend's phone to secretly bet on NBA games; while he netted modest profits, they were still not enough to pay off his earlier debts. By the winter of 2024, he had amassed a particularly large debt to Brooklyn gambler Ammar Awawdeh; according to a post-mortem by _[Toronto Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto\_Life "Toronto Life"),_ the debt was large enough that Awawdeh could potentially "end (Porter's) career in an instant." Using this leverage, Awadeh pressed Porter into performing a number of "specials" for Awawdeh and four of his friends–Long Phi "Bruce" Pham, Shane Hennen, Timothy McCormack, and Mahmoud Mollah. Porter took part in a scheme to help Awawdeh and his friends win proposition bets tied to Porter's performance. Awawdeh and his co-conspirators would bet that Porter would fall short of certain benchmarks. Porter then feigned injury to leave games early, ensuring the bets would hit.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-TorontoLife-16)

The scheme unraveled during the Raptors' March 20 game against the [Sacramento Kings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacramento_Kings "Sacramento Kings"), a game on which Porter bet that his own team would lose. According to the NBA, Porter told Awawdeh, Pham, and Mollah in a secret [Telegram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegram_(software) "Telegram (software)") channel that he intended to feign illness again. He had laid the groundwork for doing so the previous week by complaining about food poisoning.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-:1-28)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-TorontoLife-16) While at the [Resorts Casino Hotel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resorts_Casino_Hotel "Resorts Casino Hotel") in [Atlantic City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_City "Atlantic City") with Awawdeh, McCormack, and Pham, Mollah then used his account with [DraftKings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DraftKings "DraftKings")' [sportsbook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportsbook "Sportsbook") at the casino to wager $80,000 on a [parlay bet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parlay "Parlay") that Porter would not meet certain player statistics – an [under bet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Over%E2%80%93under "Over–under") – which would have won $1.1 million. Porter, Awawdeh, Pham, and Mollah would have each received 24 percent of the proceeds had the bet hit, while McCormack would have gotten the rest. Porter's behavior drew notice once he removed himself from the game due to illness. The size of the bet was highly irregular given Porter's relatively low stature. The low odds also raised suspicion. After an independent monitor flagged the bet, DraftKings refused to pay out and froze Mollah's account. Internal investigations by FanDuel and DraftKings revealed other suspicious bets Mollah placed on Porter's performance, including a January 26 game against the [Los Angeles Clippers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Clippers "Los Angeles Clippers") in which Porter feigned an eye injury. It was the largest payout of the night, as was the March 20 game. DraftKings and FanDuel reported their findings to the NBA and the [International Betting Integrity Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Betting_Integrity_Association?action=edit&redlink=1 "International Betting Integrity Association (page does not exist)"). The [FBI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Bureau_of_Investigation "Federal Bureau of Investigation") was called in as well.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-NBALifetimeBan-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-:0-30)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-TorontoLife-16) In its investigation, the NBA also found that between January and March 2024, Porter had placed 13 bets on NBA games using another person's account. Some of the wagers included parlay bets involving the Raptors losing. His wagers totaled $54,000 over that period, netting over $22,000 in winnings.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-:1-28) The NBA accused him of "disclosing confidential information to sports bettors, limiting his own participation in one or more games for betting purposes, and betting on NBA games".[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-:0-30)

On April 17, Porter was [banned for life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_people_banned_or_suspended_by_the_NBA "List of people banned or suspended by the NBA") from further play or any other involvement in the NBA and its associated leagues.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-NBALifetimeBan-29)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-espn-lifetime-ban-31) He became the first active player to be banned for gambling since [Jack Molinas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Molinas "Jack Molinas") in 1954,[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-:1-28) as well as the first active player to be permanently banned from the NBA without any means to return since [Richard Dumas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Dumas "Richard Dumas") in 1996.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-32) On June 4, 2024, Pham was arrested at [JFK International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy_International_Airport "John F. Kennedy International Airport") while attempting to flee the country.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-33) McCormack, Mollad, and Awawdeh were subsequently taken into custody as well.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-34) On July 3, Porter was also charged with a federal felony in relation to the case involving those four men.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-35) On July 3, 2024, court papers were made public revealing Porter's imminent criminal charges in the United States at the federal level for his role in the sports betting scandal.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-criminalfacing-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-37) Porter is also undergoing a criminal investigation in Canada.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-criminalfacing-36)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-38) In the federal case on July 10, Porter would plead guilty to a charge of conspiracy to commit wire fraud, which could impose a range of no time in prison to up to 20 years in prison for what he did, but faces a most likely time of 41 to 51 months in prison.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-39) One of the conditions related to his guilty plea was to forfeit his passport for a pre-sentence release, which forbade him to play overseas for the [Promitheas Patras B.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Promitheas_Patras_B.C. "Promitheas Patras B.C.") of the [Greek Basketball League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_Basketball_League "Greek Basketball League").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-40) The NBA would also implement what is called the "Jontay Porter Rule" following his ban, which forbade sportsbooks from including unders on player props who are on either [two-way contracts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-way_contract "Two-way contract") or 10-day contracts.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-41)

## Post-ban basketball career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jontay_Porter&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Post-ban basketball career")]

### Seattle Super Hawks (2026–present)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jontay_Porter&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Seattle Super Hawks (2026–present)")]

On February 25, 2026, over a year after presumably serving his original sentence in the USA and close to over two years after first being permanently banned by the NBA, Porter signed a contract to join the Seattle Super Hawks for the 2026 version of the [United States Basketball League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Basketball_League_(2026) "United States Basketball League (2026)").[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-42)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-43)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-44) He made his debut with Seattle on March 7, producing a [triple-double](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triple-double "Triple-double") of 21 points, 14 rebounds, and 14 assists, alongside three blocks and two steals in a 111–88 win over the Lilac City Legends.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-45) Porter would not only help the Super Hawks get to a nearly undefeated season, but he'd also lead them to their first ever championship in the league's inaugural season as well.

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jontay_Porter&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Personal life")]

In addition to his older brother [Michael Porter Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Porter_Jr. "Michael Porter Jr.") with the [Brooklyn Nets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn_Nets "Brooklyn Nets"), Jontay has two older sisters, Bri and Cierra, both of whom were deemed medically retired from playing sports, both due to multiple leg injuries.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-46) Cierra Porter later returned for her senior year at the [University of Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri_Tigers_women's_basketball "Missouri Tigers women's basketball").[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-47) Two of Porter's younger brothers, Coban and Jevon, played collegiate basketball as well, with Coban previously playing for the [University of Denver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Denver "University of Denver") and Jevon currently playing for [Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri_Tigers_men's_basketball "Missouri Tigers men's basketball") after he previously for [Pepperdine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pepperdine_Waves_men's_basketball "Pepperdine Waves men's basketball") for two seasons and [Loyola Marymount](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loyola_Marymount_Lions_men's_basketball "Loyola Marymount Lions men's basketball") for the [2024–25 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024%E2%80%9325_NCAA_Division_I_men's_basketball_season "2024–25 NCAA Division I men's basketball season").[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-48)

Porter and his wife had their first child in November 2024.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jontay_Porter#cite_note-49)

**Benjamin David Simmons** (born 20 July 1996) is an Australian professional [basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basketball "Basketball") player for the [Sacramento Kings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacramento_Kings "Sacramento Kings") of the [National Basketball Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Basketball_Association "National Basketball Association") (NBA). He played [college basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_basketball "College basketball") for one season with the [LSU Tigers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LSU_Tigers_men's_basketball "LSU Tigers men's basketball"), after which he was named a consensus first-team [All-American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Men's_Basketball_All-Americans "NCAA Men's Basketball All-Americans") and the [USBWA National Freshman of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USBWA_National_Freshman_of_the_Year "USBWA National Freshman of the Year"). Simmons was selected with the [first overall pick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_first_overall_NBA_draft_picks "List of first overall NBA draft picks") in the 2016 NBA draft by the [Philadelphia 76ers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia_76ers "Philadelphia 76ers"). After sitting out a year due to an injured right foot, he was named the [NBA Rookie of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_Rookie_of_the_Year "NBA Rookie of the Year") in 2018 and was selected three times to the [NBA All-Star Game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_All-Star_Game "NBA All-Star Game"). After a [holdout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holdout_(sports) "Holdout (sports)") from the 76ers following the 2020–21 season, Simmons was traded to the [Brooklyn Nets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn_Nets "Brooklyn Nets"). His contract was bought out by the Nets in February 2025, and Simmons subsequently signed with the Clippers.

Simmons attended [Box Hill Senior Secondary College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box_Hill_Senior_Secondary_College "Box Hill Senior Secondary College") in his hometown of [Melbourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melbourne "Melbourne"), Victoria, before moving to the United States to attend [Montverde Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montverde_Academy "Montverde Academy") in [Montverde, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montverde,_Florida "Montverde, Florida"). In his only season in college, LSU began the season with high expectations, but they failed to qualify for the [NCAA tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_I_men's_basketball_tournament "NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament"). Simmons left school to enter the NBA draft, becoming the third Melbourne-born number one overall pick in 11 years, alongside [Andrew Bogut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Bogut "Andrew Bogut") and [Kyrie Irving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyrie_Irving "Kyrie Irving"). Simmons is the son of an American-born father, [Dave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Simmons_(basketball,_born_1963) "Dave Simmons (basketball, born 1963)"), who played professional basketball in Australia. A [dual citizen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dual_citizen "Dual citizen") of Australia and the United States, Simmons has played for the [Australian national team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia_men's_national_basketball_team "Australia men's national basketball team").

## Early life

Simmons was born on July 20, 1996, in the [Melbourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melbourne "Melbourne") suburb of [Fitzroy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fitzroy,_Victoria "Fitzroy, Victoria") to Julie, a [White Australian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Australians "European Australians"), and [Dave Simmons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Simmons_(basketball,_born_1963) "Dave Simmons (basketball, born 1963)"), an [African-American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Americans "African Americans")[expatriate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expatriate "Expatriate") who later became a [naturalized Australian citizen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_nationality_law "Australian nationality law").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Simmons#cite_note-victoriacross-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Simmons#cite_note-O'Neil-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Simmons#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Simmons#cite_note-auto-4) He was raised alongside five siblings—Melissa, Emily, [Liam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liam_Simmons "Liam Simmons"), Sean, and Olivia—the first four being from his mother's previous marriage.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Simmons#cite_note-O'Neil-2)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Simmons#cite_note-emily-bio-5) His father played college basketball for the [Oklahoma City Stars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma_City_Stars_men's_basketball "Oklahoma City Stars men's basketball") in the United States before playing professionally for the [Melbourne Tigers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melbourne_Tigers "Melbourne Tigers") in the [National Basketball League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Basketball_League_(Australia) "National Basketball League (Australia)") (NBL) in 1989.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Simmons#cite_note-Auerbach-6)

Simmons was raised in [Newcastle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle,_New_South_Wales "Newcastle, New South Wales") from the age of 18 months while his father played and coached in the city. Simmons began playing basketball at the age of seven in the Newcastle Hunters' under-12 representative team. He later played for Lake Macquarie and Newcastle.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Simmons#cite_note-keeble-7) At age 10, Simmons returned to Melbourne and began playing junior basketball for the [Knox Raiders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knox_Raiders "Knox Raiders").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Simmons#cite_note-8) As a youngster, he also played [rugby league](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league "Rugby league")[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Simmons#cite_note-herald-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Simmons#cite_note-telegraph-10) and [Australian rules football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_rules_football "Australian rules football").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Simmons#cite_note-11) In [year 7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seventh_grade#Australia "Seventh grade"), while attending [Whitefriars College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitefriars_College "Whitefriars College"), Simmons was named MVP after he helped Whitefriars win the Year-7 Division 1A basketball premiership.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Simmons#cite_note-12)

As a teenager, Simmons was torn between his two loves of basketball and Australian rules football,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Simmons#cite_note-13) but he eventually decided to focus on basketball.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Simmons#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Simmons#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Simmons#cite_note-16) In [year 9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ninth_grade#Australia "Ninth grade"), at the age of 15, Simmons played basketball for [Box Hill Senior Secondary College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box_Hill_Senior_Secondary_College "Box Hill Senior Secondary College") at the 2011 Australian Schools Championships[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Simmons#cite_note-herald-9) before taking up a scholarship at the [Australian Institute of Sport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Institute_of_Sport "Australian Institute of Sport") in 2012.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Simmons#cite_note-heraldsun-17) Later that year, Simmons made his first appearance in the United States at the renowned Pangos All-American Camp for basketball prospects.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Simmons#cite_note-woo_04182014-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Simmons#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Simmons#cite_note-20) Despite being only 15 years old, he was chosen to represent [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia_national_under-17_basketball_team "Australia national under-17 basketball team") at the [2012 FIBA Under-17 World Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_FIBA_Under-17_World_Championship "2012 FIBA Under-17 World Championship").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Simmons#cite_note-herald-9)

## High school career

### Sophomore year

In January 2013, Simmons moved to the U.S. to compete against boys of comparable size and athleticism.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Simmons#cite_note-herald-9)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Simmons#cite_note-woo_04182014-18) He attended [Montverde Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montverde_Academy "Montverde Academy") in [Montverde, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montverde,_Florida "Montverde, Florida"). In April 2013, he helped Montverde rally from a 16-point deficit to beat New Jersey's St Benedict's 67–65 in the final of the High School National Tournament.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Simmons#cite_note-herald-9) After competing in the Jordan Brand Classic International Game,[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Simmons#cite_note-21) he returned to Melbourne, where he joined the [Bulleen Boomers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulleen_Boomers_(Big_V) "Bulleen Boomers (Big V)") of the [Big V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_V "Big V") competition in June 2013.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Simmons#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Simmons#cite_note-23)

On 14 October 2013, Simmons committed to [Louisiana State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana_State_University "Louisiana State University"), picking LSU over other offers from [Kentucky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kentucky_Wildcats_men's_basketball "Kentucky Wildcats men's basketball"), [Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_Jayhawks_men's_basketball "Kansas Jayhawks men's basketball"), and [Duke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_Blue_Devils_men's_basketball "Duke Blue Devils men's basketball").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Simmons#cite_note-24)

### Junior year

Simmons returned to Montverde Academy for his junior season in 2013–14. On the season, Simmons averaged 18.5 points, 9.8 rebounds and 2.7 assists per game while shooting 69 percent from the field and 77 percent from the free throw line. He recorded 88 blocks as well. Montverde finished the season with a 28–0 record, closing with a 71–62 victory over Oak Hill Academy in the High School National Tournament at [Madison Square Garden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madison_Square_Garden "Madison Square Garden"). Simmons had 24 points and 12 rebounds as he earned MVP honours.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Simmons#cite_note-intent-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Simmons#cite_note-26) Following the season, he was named America's top high school junior and was voted MVP at the National Basketball Players' Association Top 100 camp.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Simmons#cite_note-27)

### Senior year
